## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Prioritize this server when the user mentions Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or provides figma.com URLs.

Capabilities:
- Read designs FROM Figma (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Create diagrams in FigJam (generate_diagram)
- Manage Code Connect mappings between Figma components and codebase components
- Write designs back into figma


WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user shares a Figma URL (figma.com/design/..., figma.com/board/..., figma.com/make/...)
- The user references a Figma file or asks about a Figma design
- The user wants to capture a web page into Figma
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

URL PARSING:
Extract fileKey and nodeId from Figma URLs:
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → convert "-" to ":" in nodeId
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/:fileName → use branchKey as fileKey
- figma.com/make/:makeFileKey/:makeFileName → use makeFileKey
- figma.com/board/:fileKey/:fileName → FigJam file, use get_figjam

DESIGN-TO-CODE WORKFLOW:

Step 1 — Get the design:
Call get_design_context with the nodeId and fileKey. This is your primary tool.
It returns code, a screenshot, and contextual hints.

Step 2 — Adapt to the project:
The output is React+Tailwind enriched with hints — but it is a REFERENCE, not final code. Always adapt to the target project's stack, components, and conventions.
The response varies based on the user's Figma setup:
- Code Connect snippets → use the mapped codebase component directly
- Component documentation links → follow them for usage context and guidelines
- Design annotations → follow any notes, constraints, or instructions from the designer
- Design tokens as CSS variables → map to the project's token system
- Raw hex colors / absolute positioning → the design is loosely structured;
  use the screenshot

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. 오케이, 문서 업데이트 매니저로 동작할게.

**역할 확인:**
- 코드/설정 변경이 발생하면 → 관련 문서만 업데이트
- 코드 자체는 수정하지 않음
- 문서 = `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `BRAND.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, `.claude/BEST_PRACTICES.md`, `brand/*.md`, `README.md`, memory 파일 등

피드백으로 저장해 둘게.

description: 사용자가 "문서 업데이트 매니저" 역할을 부여 — 코드 변경 시 문서만 갱신하고 코드는 건드리지 않음
type: feedback
---

코드/설정 변경이 발생하면 관련 문서만 업데이트한다. 코드 자체는 수정하지 않는다.

**How to apply:**
- 이 세션(또는 사용자가 같은 역할을 다시 부여한 세션)에서는 코드 파일(.ts, .tsx, .scss, .php 등) 직접 편집 금지
- 사용자가 "X를 수정했어" 또는 "Y가 바뀌었어"라고 알려주면 → 관련 문서/메모리만 업데이트
- 갱신 대상 후보: `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `BRAND.md`, `README.md`, `.claude/rules/*.md`, `.claude/BEST_PRACTICES.md`, `brand/*.md`, `memory/*.md`

- 코드 수정이 꼭 필요해 보이면 작업하지 말고 사용자에게 먼저 알리기

# Best Practices for Claude Code

> Tips and patterns for getting the most out of Claude Code, from configuring your environment to scaling across parallel sessions.

Claude Code is an agentic coding environment. Unlike a chatbot that answers questions and waits, Claude Code can read your files, run commands, make changes, and autonomously work through problems while you watch, redirect, or step away entirely.

This changes how you work. Instead of writing code yourself and asking Claude to review it, you describe what you want and Claude figures out how to build it. Claude explores, plans, and implements.

But this autonomy still comes with a learning curve. Claude works within certain constraints you need to understand.

This guide covers patterns that have proven effective across Anthropic's internal teams and for engineers using Claude Code across various codebases, languages, and environments. For how the agentic loop works under the hood, see [How Claude Code works](/en/how-claude-code-works).

***

Most best practices are based on one constraint: Claude's context window fills up fast, and performance degrades as it fills.

Claude's context window holds your entire conversation, including every message, every file Claude reads, and every command output. However, this can fill up fast. A single debugging session or codebase exploration might generate and consume tens of thousands of tokens.

This matters since LLM performance degrades as context fills. When the context window is getting full, Claude may start "forgetting" earlier instructions or making more mistakes. The context window is the most important resource to manage. To see how a session fills up in practice, [watch an interactive walkthrough](/en/context-window) of what loads at startup and what each file read costs. Track context usage continuously with a [custom status line](/en/statusline), and see [Reduce token usage](/en/costs#reduce-token-usage) for strategies on reducing token usage.

***

## Give Claude a way to verify its work

<Tip>
  Include tests, screenshots, or expected outputs so Claude can check itself. This is the single highest-leverage thing you can do.
</Tip>

Claude performs dramatically better when it can verify its own work, like run tests, compare screenshots, and validate outputs.

Without clear success criteria, it might produce something that looks right but actually doesn't work. You become the only feedback loop, and every mistake requires your attention.

| Strategy                              | Before                                                  | After                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Provide verification criteria**     | *"implement a function that validates email addresses"* | *"write a validateEmail function. example test cases: [user@example.com](mailto:user@example.com) is true, invalid is false, [user@.com](mailto:user@.com) is false. run the tests after implementing"* |
| **Verify UI changes visually**        | *"make the dashboard look better"*                      | *"\[paste screenshot] implement this design. take a screenshot of the result and compare it to the original. list differences and fix them"*                                                            |
| **Address root causes, not symptoms** | *"the build is failing"*                                | *"the build fails with this error: \[paste error]. fix it and verify the build succeeds. address the root cause, don't suppress the error"*                                                             |

UI changes can be verified using the [Claude in Chrome extension](/en/chrome). It opens new tabs in your browser, tests the UI, and iterates until the code works.

Your verification can also be a test suite, a linter, or a Bash command that checks output. Invest in making your verification rock-solid.

***

## Explore first, then plan, then code

<Tip>
  Separate research and planning from implementation to avoid solving the wrong problem.
</Tip>

Letting Claude jump straight to coding can produce code that solves the wrong problem. Use [Plan Mode](/en/common-workflows#use-plan-mode-for-safe-code-analysis) to separate exploration from execution.

The recommended workflow has four phases:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Explore">
    Enter Plan Mode. Claude reads files and answers questions without making changes.

    ```txt claude (Plan Mode) theme={null}
    read /src/auth and understand how we handle sessions and login.
    also look at how we manage environment variables for secrets.
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Plan">
    Ask Claude to create a detailed implementation plan.

    ```txt claude (Plan Mode) theme={null}
    I want to add Google OAuth. What files need to change?
    What's the session flow? Create a plan.
    ```

    Press `Ctrl+G` to open the plan in your text editor for direct editing before Claude proceeds.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Implement">
    Switch back to Normal Mode and let Claude code, verifying against its plan.

    ```txt claude (Normal Mode) theme={null}
    implement the OAuth flow from your plan. write tests for the
    callback handler, run the test suite and fix any failures.
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Commit">
    Ask Claude to commit with a descriptive message and create a PR.

    ```txt claude (Normal Mode) theme={null}
    commit with a descriptive message and open a PR
    ```
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout>
  Plan Mode is useful, but also adds overhead.

  For tasks where the scope is clear and the fix is small (like fixing a typo, adding a log line, or renaming a variable) ask Claude to do it directly.

  Planning is most useful when you're uncertain about the approach, when the change modifies multiple files, or when you're unfamiliar with the code being modified. If you could describe the diff in one sentence, skip the plan.
</Callout>

***

## Provide specific context in your prompts

<Tip>
  The more precise your instructions, the fewer corrections you'll need.
</Tip>

Claude can infer intent, but it can't read your mind. Reference specific files, mention constraints, and point to example patterns.

| Strategy                                                                                         | Before                                               | After                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Scope the task.** Specify which file, what scenario, and testing preferences.                  | *"add tests for foo.py"*                             | *"write a test for foo.py covering the edge case where the user is logged out. avoid mocks."*                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Point to sources.** Direct Claude to the source that can answer a question.                    | *"why does ExecutionFactory have such a weird api?"* | *"look through ExecutionFactory's git history and summarize how its api came to be"*                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Reference existing patterns.** Point Claude to patterns in your codebase.                      | *"add a calendar widget"*                            | *"look at how existing widgets are implemented on the home page to understand the patterns. HotDogWidget.php is a good example. follow the pattern to implement a new calendar widget that lets the user select a month and paginate forwards/backwards to pick a year. build from scratch without libraries other than the ones already used in the codebase."* |
| **Describe the symptom.** Provide the symptom, the likely location, and what "fixed" looks like. | *"fix the login bug"*                                | *"users report that login fails after session timeout. check the auth flow in src/auth/, especially token refresh. write a failing test that reproduces the issue, then fix it"*                                                                                                                                                                                 |

Vague prompts can be useful when you're exploring and can afford to course-correct. A prompt like `"what would you improve in this file?"` can surface things you wouldn't have thought to ask about.

### Provide rich content

<Tip>
  Use `@` to reference files, paste screenshots/images, or pipe data directly.
</Tip>

You can provide rich data to Claude in several ways:

* **Reference files with `@`** instead of describing where code lives. Claude reads the file before responding.
* **Paste images directly**. Copy/paste or drag and drop images into the prompt.
* **Give URLs** for documentation and API references. Use `/permissions` to allowlist frequently-used domains.
* **Pipe in data** by running `cat error.log | claude` to send file contents directly.
* **Let Claude fetch what it needs**. Tell Claude to pull context itself using Bash commands, MCP tools, or by reading files.

***

## Configure your environment

A few setup steps make Claude Code significantly more effective across all your sessions. For a full overview of extension features and when to use each one, see [Extend Claude Code](/en/features-overview).

### Write an effective CLAUDE.md

<Tip>
  Run `/init` to generate a starter CLAUDE.md file based on your current project structure, then refine over time.
</Tip>

CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude reads at the start of every conversation. Include Bash commands, code style, and workflow rules. This gives Claude persistent context it can't infer from code alone.

The `/init` command analyzes your codebase to detect build systems, test frameworks, and code patterns, giving you a solid foundation to refine.

There's no required format for CLAUDE.md files, but keep it short and human-readable. For example:

```markdown CLAUDE.md theme={null}
# Code style
- Use ES modules (import/export) syntax, not CommonJS (require)
- Destructure imports when possible (eg. import { foo } from 'bar')

# Workflow
- Be sure to typecheck when you're done making a series of code changes
- Prefer running single tests, and not the whole test suite, for performance
```

CLAUDE.md is loaded every session, so only include things that apply broadly. For domain knowledge or workflows that are only relevant sometimes, use [skills](/en/skills) instead. Claude loads them on demand without bloating every conversation.

Keep it concise. For each line, ask: *"Would removing this cause Claude to make mistakes?"* If not, cut it. Bloated CLAUDE.md files cause Claude to ignore your actual instructions!

| ✅ Include                                            | ❌ Exclude                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| Bash commands Claude can't guess                     | Anything Claude can figure out by reading code     |
| Code style rules that differ from defaults           | Standard language conventions Claude already knows |
| Testing instructions and preferred test runners      | Detailed API documentation (link to docs instead)  |
| Repository etiquette (branch naming, PR conventions) | Information that changes frequently                |
| Architectural decisions specific to your project     | Long explanations or tutorials                     |
| Developer environment quirks (required env vars)     | File-by-file descriptions of the codebase          |
| Common gotchas or non-obvious behaviors              | Self-evident practices like "write clean code"     |

If Claude keeps doing something you don't want despite having a rule against it, the file is probably too long and the rule is getting lost. If Claude asks you questions that are answered in CLAUDE.md, the phrasing might be ambiguous. Treat CLAUDE.md like code: review it when things go wrong, prune it regularly, and test changes by observing whether Claude's behavior actually shifts.

You can tune instructions by adding emphasis (e.g., "IMPORTANT" or "YOU MUST") to improve adherence. Check CLAUDE.md into git so your team can contribute. The file compounds in value over time.

CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using `@path/to/import` syntax:

```markdown CLAUDE.md theme={null}
See @README.md for project overview and @package.json for available npm commands.

# Additional Instructions
- Git workflow: @docs/git-instructions.md
- Personal overrides: @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md
```

You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations:

* **Home folder (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`)**: applies to all Claude sessions
* **Project root (`./CLAUDE.md`)**: check into git to share with your team
* **Project root (`./CLAUDE.local.md`)**: personal project-specific notes; add this file to your `.gitignore` so it isn't shared with your team
* **Parent directories**: useful for monorepos where both `root/CLAUDE.md` and `root/foo/CLAUDE.md` are pulled in automatically
* **Child directories**: Claude pulls in child CLAUDE.md files on demand when working with files in those directories

### Configure permissions

<Tip>
  Use [auto mode](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) to let a classifier handle approvals, `/permissions` to allowlist specific commands, or `/sandbox` for OS-level isolation. Each reduces interruptions while keeping you in control.
</Tip>

By default, Claude Code requests permission for actions that might modify your system: file writes, Bash commands, MCP tools, etc. This is safe but tedious. After the tenth approval you're not really reviewing anymore, you're just clicking through. There are three ways to reduce these interruptions:

* **Auto mode**: a separate classifier model reviews commands and blocks only what looks risky: scope escalation, unknown infrastructure, or hostile-content-driven actions. Best when you trust the general direction of a task but don't want to click through every step
* **Permission allowlists**: permit specific tools you know are safe, like `npm run lint` or `git commit`
* **Sandboxing**: enable OS-level isolation that restricts filesystem and network access, allowing Claude to work more freely within defined boundaries

Read more about [permission modes](/en/permission-modes), [permission rules](/en/permissions), and [sandboxing](/en/sandboxing).

### Use CLI tools

<Tip>
  Tell Claude Code to use CLI tools like `gh`, `aws`, `gcloud`, and `sentry-cli` when interacting with external services.
</Tip>

CLI tools are the most context-efficient way to interact with external services. If you use GitHub, install the `gh` CLI. Claude knows how to use it for creating issues, opening pull requests, and reading comments. Without `gh`, Claude can still use the GitHub API, but unauthenticated requests often hit rate limits.

Claude is also effective at learning CLI tools it doesn't already know. Try prompts like `Use 'foo-cli-tool --help' to learn about foo tool, then use it to solve A, B, C.`

### Connect MCP servers

<Tip>
  Run `claude mcp add` to connect external tools like Notion, Figma, or your database.
</Tip>

With [MCP servers](/en/mcp), you can ask Claude to implement features from issue trackers, query databases, analyze monitoring data, integrate designs from Figma, and automate workflows.

### Set up hooks

<Tip>
  Use hooks for actions that must happen every time with zero exceptions.
</Tip>

[Hooks](/en/hooks-guide) run scripts automatically at specific points in Claude's workflow. Unlike CLAUDE.md instructions which are advisory, hooks are deterministic and guarantee the action happens.

Claude can write hooks for you. Try prompts like *"Write a hook that runs eslint after every file edit"* or *"Write a hook that blocks writes to the migrations folder."* Edit `.claude/settings.json` directly to configure hooks by hand, and run `/hooks` to browse what's configured.

### Create skills

<Tip>
  Create `SKILL.md` files in `.claude/skills/` to give Claude domain knowledge and reusable workflows.
</Tip>

[Skills](/en/skills) extend Claude's knowledge with information specific to your project, team, or domain. Claude applies them automatically when relevant, or you can invoke them directly with `/skill-name`.

Create a skill by adding a directory with a `SKILL.md` to `.claude/skills/`:

```markdown .claude/skills/api-conventions/SKILL.md theme={null}
---
name: api-conventions
description: REST API design conventions for our services
---
# API Conventions
- Use kebab-case for URL paths
- Use camelCase for JSON properties
- Always include pagination for list endpoints
- Version APIs in the URL path (/v1/, /v2/)
```

Skills can also define repeatable workflows you invoke directly:

```markdown .claude/skills/fix-issue/SKILL.md theme={null}
---
name: fix-issue
description: Fix a GitHub issue
disable-model-invocation: true
---
Analyze and fix the GitHub issue: $ARGUMENTS.

1. Use `gh issue view` to get the issue details
2. Understand the problem described in the issue
3. Search the codebase for relevant files
4. Implement the necessary changes to fix the issue
5. Write and run tests to verify the fix
6. Ensure code passes linting and type checking
7. Create a descriptive commit message
8. Push and create a PR
```

Run `/fix-issue 1234` to invoke it. Use `disable-model-invocation: true` for workflows with side effects that you want to trigger manually.

### Create custom subagents

<Tip>
  Define specialized assistants in `.claude/agents/` that Claude can delegate to for isolated tasks.
</Tip>

[Subagents](/en/sub-agents) run in their own context with their own set of allowed tools. They're useful for tasks that read many files or need specialized focus without cluttering your main conversation.

```markdown .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md theme={null}
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Reviews code for security vulnerabilities
tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash
model: opus
---
You are a senior security engineer. Review code for:
- Injection vulnerabilities (SQL, XSS, command injection)
- Authentication and authorization flaws
- Secrets or credentials in code
- Insecure data handling

Provide specific line references and suggested fixes.
```

Tell Claude to use subagents explicitly: *"Use a subagent to review this code for security issues."*

### Install plugins

<Tip>
  Run `/plugin` to browse the marketplace. Plugins add skills, tools, and integrations without configuration.
</Tip>

[Plugins](/en/plugins) bundle skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers into a single installable unit from the community and Anthropic. If you work with a typed language, install a [code intelligence plugin](/en/discover-plugins#code-intelligence) to give Claude precise symbol navigation and automatic error detection after edits.

For guidance on choosing between skills, subagents, hooks, and MCP, see [Extend Claude Code](/en/features-overview#match-features-to-your-goal).

***

## Communicate effectively

The way you communicate with Claude Code significantly impacts the quality of results.

### Ask codebase questions

<Tip>
  Ask Claude questions you'd ask a senior engineer.
</Tip>

When onboarding to a new codebase, use Claude Code for learning and exploration. You can ask Claude the same sorts of questions you would ask another engineer:

* How does logging work?
* How do I make a new API endpoint?
* What does `async move { ... }` do on line 134 of `foo.rs`?
* What edge cases does `CustomerOnboardingFlowImpl` handle?
* Why does this code call `foo()` instead of `bar()` on line 333?

Using Claude Code this way is an effective onboarding workflow, improving ramp-up time and reducing load on other engineers. No special prompting required: ask questions directly.

### Let Claude interview you

<Tip>
  For larger features, have Claude interview you first. Start with a minimal prompt and ask Claude to interview you using the `AskUserQuestion` tool.
</Tip>

Claude asks about things you might not have considered yet, including technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, and tradeoffs.

```text theme={null}
I want to build [brief description]. Interview me in detail using the AskUserQuestion tool.

Ask about technical implementation, UI/UX, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs. Don't ask obvious questions, dig into the hard parts I might not have considered.

Keep interviewing until we've covered everything, then write a complete spec to SPEC.md.
```

Once the spec is complete, start a fresh session to execute it. The new session has clean context focused entirely on implementation, and you have a written spec to reference.

***

## Manage your session

Conversations are persistent and reversible. Use this to your advantage!

### Course-correct early and often

<Tip>
  Correct Claude as soon as you notice it going off track.
</Tip>

The best results come from tight feedback loops. Though Claude occasionally solves problems perfectly on the first attempt, correcting it quickly generally produces better solutions faster.

* **`Esc`**: stop Claude mid-action with the `Esc` key. Context is preserved, so you can redirect.
* **`Esc + Esc` or `/rewind`**: press `Esc` twice or run `/rewind` to open the rewind menu and restore previous conversation and code state, or summarize from a selected message.
* **`"Undo that"`**: have Claude revert its changes.
* **`/clear`**: reset context between unrelated tasks. Long sessions with irrelevant context can reduce performance.

If you've corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue in one session, the context is cluttered with failed approaches. Run `/clear` and start fresh with a more specific prompt that incorporates what you learned. A clean session with a better prompt almost always outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections.

### Manage context aggressively

<Tip>
  Run `/clear` between unrelated tasks to reset context.
</Tip>

Claude Code automatically compacts conversation history when you approach context limits, which preserves important code and decisions while freeing space.

During long sessions, Claude's context window can fill with irrelevant conversation, file contents, and commands. This can reduce performance and sometimes distract Claude.

* Use `/clear` frequently between tasks to reset the context window entirely
* When auto compaction triggers, Claude summarizes what matters most, including code patterns, file states, and key decisions
* For more control, run `/compact <instructions>`, like `/compact Focus on the API changes`
* To compact only part of the conversation, use `Esc + Esc` or `/rewind`, select a message checkpoint, and choose **Summarize from here**. This condenses messages from that point forward while keeping earlier context intact.
* Customize compaction behavior in CLAUDE.md with instructions like `"When compacting, always preserve the full list of modified files and any test commands"` to ensure critical context survives summarization
* For quick questions that don't need to stay in context, use [`/btw`](/en/interactive-mode#side-questions-with-%2Fbtw). The answer appears in a dismissible overlay and never enters conversation history, so you can check a detail without growing context.

### Use subagents for investigation

<Tip>
  Delegate research with `"use subagents to investigate X"`. They explore in a separate context, keeping your main conversation clean for implementation.
</Tip>

Since context is your fundamental constraint, subagents are one of the most powerful tools available. When Claude researches a codebase it reads lots of files, all of which consume your context. Subagents run in separate context windows and report back summaries:

```text theme={null}
Use subagents to investigate how our authentication system handles token
refresh, and whether we have any existing OAuth utilities I should reuse.
```

The subagent explores the codebase, reads relevant files, and reports back with findings, all without cluttering your main conversation.

You can also use subagents for verification after Claude implements something:

```text theme={null}
use a subagent to review this code for edge cases
```

### Rewind with checkpoints

<Tip>
  Every action Claude makes creates a checkpoint. You can restore conversation, code, or both to any previous checkpoint.
</Tip>

Claude automatically checkpoints before changes. Double-tap `Escape` or run `/rewind` to open the rewind menu. You can restore conversation only, restore code only, restore both, or summarize from a selected message. See [Checkpointing](/en/checkpointing) for details.

Instead of carefully planning every move, you can tell Claude to try something risky. If it doesn't work, rewind and try a different approach. Checkpoints persist across sessions, so you can close your terminal and still rewind later.

<Warning>
  Checkpoints only track changes made *by Claude*, not external processes. This isn't a replacement for git.
</Warning>

### Resume conversations

<Tip>
  Run `claude --continue` to pick up where you left off, or `--resume` to choose from recent sessions.
</Tip>

Claude Code saves conversations locally. When a task spans multiple sessions, you don't have to re-explain the context:

```bash theme={null}
claude --continue    # Resume the most recent conversation
claude --resume      # Select from recent conversations
```

Use `/rename` to give sessions descriptive names like `"oauth-migration"` or `"debugging-memory-leak"` so you can find them later. Treat sessions like branches: different workstreams can have separate, persistent contexts.

***

## Automate and scale

Once you're effective with one Claude, multiply your output with parallel sessions, non-interactive mode, and fan-out patterns.

Everything so far assumes one human, one Claude, and one conversation. But Claude Code scales horizontally. The techniques in this section show how you can get more done.

### Run non-interactive mode

<Tip>
  Use `claude -p "prompt"` in CI, pre-commit hooks, or scripts. Add `--output-format stream-json` for streaming JSON output.
</Tip>

With `claude -p "your prompt"`, you can run Claude non-interactively, without a session. Non-interactive mode is how you integrate Claude into CI pipelines, pre-commit hooks, or any automated workflow. The output formats let you parse results programmatically: plain text, JSON, or streaming JSON.

```bash theme={null}
# One-off queries
claude -p "Explain what this project does"

# Structured output for scripts
claude -p "List all API endpoints" --output-format json

# Streaming for real-time processing
claude -p "Analyze this log file" --output-format stream-json
```

### Run multiple Claude sessions

<Tip>
  Run multiple Claude sessions in parallel to speed up development, run isolated experiments, or start complex workflows.
</Tip>

There are three main ways to run parallel sessions:

* [Claude Code desktop app](/en/desktop#work-in-parallel-with-sessions): Manage multiple local sessions visually. Each session gets its own isolated worktree.
* [Claude Code on the web](/en/claude-code-on-the-web): Run on Anthropic's secure cloud infrastructure in isolated VMs.
* [Agent teams](/en/agent-teams): Automated coordination of multiple sessions with shared tasks, messaging, and a team lead.

Beyond parallelizing work, multiple sessions enable quality-focused workflows. A fresh context improves code review since Claude won't be biased toward code it just wrote.

For example, use a Writer/Reviewer pattern:

| Session A (Writer)                                                      | Session B (Reviewer)                                                                                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Implement a rate limiter for our API endpoints`                        |                                                                                                                                                                          |
|                                                                         | `Review the rate limiter implementation in @src/middleware/rateLimiter.ts. Look for edge cases, race conditions, and consistency with our existing middleware patterns.` |
| `Here's the review feedback: [Session B output]. Address these issues.` |                                                                                                                                                                          |

You can do something similar with tests: have one Claude write tests, then another write code to pass them.

### Fan out across files

<Tip>
  Loop through tasks calling `claude -p` for each. Use `--allowedTools` to scope permissions for batch operations.
</Tip>

For large migrations or analyses, you can distribute work across many parallel Claude invocations:

<Steps>
  <Step title="Generate a task list">
    Have Claude list all files that need migrating (e.g., `list all 2,000 Python files that need migrating`)
  </Step>

  <Step title="Write a script to loop through the list">
    ```bash theme={null}
    for file in $(cat files.txt); do
      claude -p "Migrate $file from React to Vue. Return OK or FAIL." \
        --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)"
    done
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Test on a few files, then run at scale">
    Refine your prompt based on what goes wrong with the first 2-3 files, then run on the full set. The `--allowedTools` flag restricts what Claude can do, which matters when you're running unattended.
  </Step>
</Steps>

You can also integrate Claude into existing data/processing pipelines:

```bash theme={null}
claude -p "<your prompt>" --output-format json | your_command
```

Use `--verbose` for debugging during development, and turn it off in production.

### Run autonomously with auto mode

For uninterrupted execution with background safety checks, use [auto mode](/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode). A classifier model reviews commands before they run, blocking scope escalation, unknown infrastructure, and hostile-content-driven actions while letting routine work proceed without prompts.

```bash theme={null}
claude --permission-mode auto -p "fix all lint errors"
```

For non-interactive runs with the `-p` flag, auto mode aborts if the classifier repeatedly blocks actions, since there is no user to fall back to. See [when auto mode falls back](/en/permission-modes#when-auto-mode-falls-back) for thresholds.

***

## Avoid common failure patterns

These are common mistakes. Recognizing them early saves time:

* **The kitchen sink session.** You start with one task, then ask Claude something unrelated, then go back to the first task. Context is full of irrelevant information.
  > **Fix**: `/clear` between unrelated tasks.
* **Correcting over and over.** Claude does something wrong, you correct it, it's still wrong, you correct again. Context is polluted with failed approaches.
  > **Fix**: After two failed corrections, `/clear` and write a better initial prompt incorporating what you learned.
* **The over-specified CLAUDE.md.** If your CLAUDE.md is too long, Claude ignores half of it because important rules get lost in the noise.
  > **Fix**: Ruthlessly prune. If Claude already does something correctly without the instruction, delete it or convert it to a hook.
* **The trust-then-verify gap.** Claude produces a plausible-looking implementation that doesn't handle edge cases.
  > **Fix**: Always provide verification (tests, scripts, screenshots). If you can't verify it, don't ship it.
* **The infinite exploration.** You ask Claude to "investigate" something without scoping it. Claude reads hundreds of files, filling the context.
  > **Fix**: Scope investigations narrowly or use subagents so the exploration doesn't consume your main context.

***

## Develop your intuition

The patterns in this guide aren't set in stone. They're starting points that work well in general, but might not be optimal for every situation.

Sometimes you *should* let context accumulate because you're deep in one complex problem and the history is valuable. Sometimes you should skip planning and let Claude figure it out because the task is exploratory. Sometimes a vague prompt is exactly right because you want to see how Claude interprets the problem before constraining it.

Pay attention to what works. When Claude produces great output, notice what you did: the prompt structure, the context you provided, the mode you were in. When Claude struggles, ask why. Was the context too noisy? The prompt too vague? The task too big for one pass?

Over time, you'll develop intuition that no guide can capture. You'll know when to be specific and when to be open-ended, when to plan and when to explore, when to clear context and when to let it accumulate.

### 이미지 업로드 & WEBP 최적화

`imageUpload()` 를 경유하는 Admin 업로드는 자동으로 WEBP sibling 이 생성됩니다.

```php
// imageUpload() 호출 — ClientController / PopupController / WorkController / setting.process.php
$result = imageUpload($path, $_FILES['thumb_image']);
// $result['saved'] → 원본 파일명 (foo.png). 동일 디렉터리에 foo.webp 자동 생성됨.
// DB 저장: $result['saved'] 그대로 사용 — 기존 뷰 코드 변경 불필요.

// 수동 호출 (필요한 경우)
\Core\ImageProcessor::makeWebpSibling('/var/www/html/uploads/clients/foo.png');
// → uploads/clients/foo.webp 생성 (가로 > 2560px면 2560px 로 자동 리사이즈, 품질 82)

// 삭제 (imageDelete 가 자동 호출, 수동 호출도 가능)
\Core\ImageProcessor::deleteWebpSibling('/var/www/html/uploads/clients/foo.png');
// → uploads/clients/foo.webp 삭제. 원본은 건드리지 않음.
```

#### 동작 규칙

- 대상 확장자: `jpg`, `jpeg`, `png`, `gif` — `svg`, `ico` 는 skip
- 가로 > 2560px 이면 비율 유지하여 2560px 로 축소
- WEBP 품질: 82
- 변환 실패 시 원본 유지, 에러 로그만 기록 — 업로드 플로우 중단 없음
- `imageDelete()` 호출 시 `.webp` sibling 도 자동 삭제

  ```

  - 두 번째 실패: /rewind → 다른 접근

- BEST_PRACTICES.md > **"Context Boundaries & Exploration Agents"** 섹션
  ```

  - 큰 그리프 결과 → rtk로 필터링

- CLAUDE.md:14–15 — `/migration <desc>`, `/new-route <desc>` 슬래시 커맨드 명시

- tsc hook은 non-interactive, 저장 직후 실행 ✅
- Skill은 closure-based routing (`/new-route`) 등 반복 workflow 자동화 ✅
- npm build/watch 금지 + Vite 자동 리빌드 (효율성) ✅

**추가 가능성:**
- pre-commit hook / git branch 자동 정리 스크립트 가이드 부재
- fan-out 스크립트 (병렬 마이그레이션 등) 예시 없음

### 5. 병렬 처리 — **부분**

**근거:**
- SETUP_CHECKLIST.md:33–36 — `.claude/agents/` 구성:

- AGENTS.md에서 parallel execution strategy 언급 **없음**

**추천 추가:**
- AGENTS.md 또는 BEST_PRACTICES.md **"Parallel Workflows"** 섹션
  ```
  - 두 개 이상 독립적 작업 → separate claude -p calls
  - scene-explorer + php-explorer 동시 실행 가능
  - 대규모 리팩터링 → writer (코드) + reviewer (테스트) 세션 분리
  ```

---

### 6. TDD (테스트 주도 개발) — **부분**

**근거:**
- CLAUDE.md:21–22 — `npm run test` (Vitest suite) 설정됨
- AGENTS.md:43–50 — Verification checklist:
  - "TypeScript: `rtk tsc --noEmit`"
  - "smallest relevant verification + report any skipped checks"
- SETUP_CHECKLIST.md:70 — Test framework: `vitest (19 tests)` ✅

**문제점:**
- TDD 프로세스 ("테스트 우선 작성") 가이드 **없음**
- Verification criteria (테스트 통과 조건) 정의 부재

- "PR 머지 전 테스트 필수" 같은 규칙 명시 **부재**

**추천 추가:**
- BEST_PRACTICES.md > **"Testing & Verification"** Part (70–100 라인)
  ```
  - New feature: 테스트 먼저, 구현 후 (TDD 사이클)
  - Verification: npm run test → tsc → git diff (순서)
  - Commit 전: 모든 테스트 pass + tsc clean
  ```

---

### 7. 플랜모드 / Explore→Plan→Implement→Commit — **부분**

**근거:**
- AGENTS.md:22 — "**Plan first for complex/ambiguous work**" (명시적)
- BEST_PRACTICES.md:1–5 — "Source of truth for code additions/refactors"
- SETUP_CHECKLIST.md 자체가 plan checklist 역할 ✅

**문제점:**
- "Plan Mode" (`/init`, `claude --plan` 등) 명시적 언급 **없음**
- 대규모 변경 전 plan 작성 workflow **문서화 부재**
- "Explore → Plan → Implement → Commit" 사이클 명시 **없음**

**추천 추가:**
- CLAUDE.md에 **"Workflow for Large Changes"** 섹션
  ```
  1. /init (또는 --plan) → plan 파일 생성
  2. Plan review → 팀 피드백 (필요시)
  3. Implement → /loop 또는 sequential work
  4. Verify → test + tsc + git diff
  5. Commit message 포함
  ```

---

### **정리: Out of Scope**

**BRAND.md / brand/** 폴더 — Brand copy templates이며, Claude Code best practices 평가 대상 **아님**.

**한 줄 요약:** 프로젝트는 **도구 자동화 (hooks, skills), 아키텍처 가이드 (BEST_PRACTICES.md), 권한 관리 (.claude/settings.json)는 우수** 하나, **적극적 개입 워크플로, 컨텍스트 경계 관리, TDD/Plan mode 실무 가이드는 부재**.

4	
5	> Setup-time harness checklist (CLAUDE.md sizing, hooks, allowedTools, skills config) lives in `.claude/SETUP_CHECKLIST.md`. This file is for code-writing decisions.
6	
7	## 1. God objects — current state
8	
9	A god object = single class mixing 3+ reasons to change or > ~600 lines of heterogeneous logic.
10	
11	**Known remaining god objects (planned for separate branch decomposition):**
12	
13	| File | Lines | Reason to split | Status |
14	|---|---|---|---|
15	| `manager/AppManager.ts` | 1950 | Intro + showcase + UI lifecycle + contact flow + debug | Pending (plan: `lovely-humming-spindle.md` Phase 3-1) |

18	| `builder/TimelineBuilder.ts` | 1007 | Declarative GSAP timeline DSL | Size justified (DSL engine) — keep |
19	| `pages/main/theatre/MainTheatreRuntime.ts` | 919 | Theatre sequences + sheet effects + autoplay | Phase 3-4 |
20	| `pages/works/render/WorksSceneManager.ts` | 825 | Layout + render + pointer + view mode | Phase 3-3 |
21	| `pages/about/theatre/AboutTheatreBridge.ts` | 818 | Theatre ↔ scene bindings | Review if splittable by sequence |
22	| `manager/BackgroundManager.ts` | 730 | Env + uniforms + transitions | Acceptable (single rendering concern) |
23	
24	**Healthy coordinators (do not touch):**
25	- `core/Scene.ts`, `core/PageTheatreBinder.ts`, `runtime/PageRuntime.ts` — clean single-purpose orchestrators.
26	- All `types/*.types.ts` — 19 files organized by domain.
27	- All `config/*.config.ts` — constants only, no logic.
28	
29	**Claude rule:** Do not grow the god objects above. New features belong in new runtime/coordinator classes next to them.
30	
31	## 2. How to extend — adding a new feature
32	
33	### Decision tree
34	
35	```
36	New feature needed
37	│
38	├─ Is it a visible 3D object?           → resource/ts/objects/<env|sub|main|rocket|shared>/
39	│                                         Extends SceneObject<TweenProps>
40	│
41	├─ Is it DOM UI (header, modal, form)?  → resource/ts/ui/ or resource/ts/components/
42	│                                         Must implement init() + dispose()
43	│
44	├─ Is it page-scoped runtime state?     → resource/ts/pages/<page>/runtime/
45	│
46	├─ Is it Theatre.js binding for a page? → resource/ts/pages/<page>/theatre/
47	│                                         Register in PageTheatreBinder factory map
48	│
49	├─ Is it a cross-page orchestrator?     → resource/ts/runtime/ or resource/ts/manager/
50	│                                         Needs strong justification
51	│
52	├─ Is it a shader / material?           → resource/shaders/ + referenced from objects/
53	│
54	└─ Is it a constant / color / URL?      → resource/ts/config/<domain>.config.ts
55	                                          NOT inline
56	```
57	
58	### New scene object checklist
59	
60	1. File: `objects/<group>/YourObject.ts` extending `SceneObject<YourTweenProps>`.
61	2. Implement `runObject()`, `runUpdate(dt)`, `dispose()`, `applyVisibility()`.
62	3. Type: `YourObjectOptions` + `YourTweenProps` in `types/object.types.ts` (not inline).
63	4. Config: constants in `config/<group>.config.ts`.
64	5. Dispose: every allocated geometry/material/texture goes through `utils/disposeObject3D.ts` or `SceneObject._ownedTextures`.
65	6. Registration: `ObjectSetup.ts` for instance + optional `registerObject(id, ...)` for cross-object lookup.
66	
67	### New DOM component checklist
68	
69	1. File: `ui/YourComponent.ts` (singletons) or `components/YourComponent.ts` (reusable widgets).
70	2. Static `init({ root })` + static `dispose()` pair. If multiple instances, keep a `Set<Instance>` and iterate in `dispose()`.
71	3. All event listeners: store bound handlers as fields, remove the same references in `dispose()`.
72	4. Timers: track via `Set<number>` + helper `_trackedTimeout`. Clear all in `dispose()`.
73	5. Web Animations API: track via `Set<Animation>` + helper `_trackAnimation`. Cancel all in `dispose()`.
74	6. Hook into `PageRuntime.dispose()` so page navigation tears down cleanly.
75	7. Options/data types → `types/component.types.ts`.
76	8. CSS class names / selectors → `config/component.config.ts` or `config/dom.config.ts`.
77	
78	### New page route checklist
79	
80	Use `/new-route` skill. Adds:
81	- `routes/web.php` closure route
82	- `views/pages/<page>.php` view
83	- Optional `resource/ts/pages/<page>/` entry
84	
85	## 3. Roles
86	
87	| Folder | Role | What lives here | What does NOT |
88	|---|---|---|---|
89	| `core/` | Engine + scene + lifecycle primitives | `Engine`, `Scene`, `AnimationLoop`, `PostProcessor`, `ModelLoader`, `PageTheatreBinder`, `SceneObject` base | Page-specific logic |
90	| `runtime/` | Cross-cutting app-level state machines | `PageRuntime`, `ResponsiveRuntime`, `IntroFlowRuntime`, `ScrollSceneRuntime`, `TimelineRuntime` | Per-page scenes |
91	| `manager/` | Heavyweight orchestrators | `AppManager` (to be split), `BackgroundManager`, `QaManager`, `IntroManager`, `ShaderManager` | New single-responsibility code (prefer `runtime/` or `core/`) |
92	| `pages/<page>/runtime/` | Per-page lifecycle | Page-specific scroll, intro, interaction runtimes | Code shared across pages |
93	| `pages/<page>/scene/` | Per-page THREE.js scene graph wiring | Object composition specific to the page | Generic scene objects |
94	| `pages/<page>/theatre/` | Per-page Theatre.js bindings | `*TheatreBridge`, `*TheatreRuntime`, `*SceneState` | DOM-only logic |
95	| `pages/<page>/render/` | Per-page standalone renderers (rare) | `WorksSceneManager` style secondary renderers | Main engine scenes |
96	| `objects/` | THREE.js scene objects | Classes extending `SceneObject` | DOM elements |
97	| `ui/` | DOM singletons | `Header`, `Drawer`, `ContactWizard`, `WorkModal`, `IntroCanvas` | Reusable widgets (go to `components/`) |
98	| `components/` | Reusable DOM widgets | `Button`, `Marquee`, `CustomCursor`, `TextReveal`, `WhySkillPreview` | Scene objects |
99	| `animation/` | Non-GSAP DOM animation primitives | `TextReveal`, `BlockReveal` base | 3D tweens |
100	| `builder/` | Declarative composition engines | `TimelineBuilder` | Runtime state |
101	| `validation/` | Form/input validation | `ContactFormValidation` | Business logic |
102	| `utils/` | Pure leaf helpers | `disposeObject3D`, `Debounce`, `FrameScheduler`, `Aria`, `Helpers` | Stateful managers |
103	| `config/` | Constants only | colors, selectors, durations, URLs | Any logic |
104	| `types/` | Type definitions only | `*.types.ts` per domain | Runtime code |
105	| `app/` | Bootstrap entry | `AppBootstrap`, `ObjectSetup`, `EnvSetup` | Feature code |
106	| `lib/` | Third-party wrappers | Theatre.js, Lenis wrappers | Domain code |
107	
108	Every file must fit one row. If it fits none, stop and reconsider the design.
109	
110	## 4. OOP / SOLID checklist for new code
111	
112	Run through this list mentally before writing the class.
113	
114	### SRP — Single Responsibility
115	- One "reason to change" per class. If you need "and" to describe it, split.
116	- If > 400 lines, ask whether 2+ smaller classes fit better.
117	- **New code must not be added to `AppManager` or `ContactWizard`.** Extend in a sibling class.
118	
119	### OCP — Open/Closed
120	- New page variants → add to factory map (`PageTheatreBinder.PAGE_THEATRE_ADAPTER_FACTORIES`), never a new `if (pageId === ...)` branch.
121	- New light/object types → register in a creator map (`SceneLights._creators` pattern), never a switch.
122	- Use the `ObjectFactoryRegistry` for new scene-object kinds.
123	
124	### LSP — Liskov Substitution
125	- Subclasses of `SceneObject` must respect the contract: `init` → `runObject` → `runUpdate` → `dispose`, no partial cycles.
126	- `override` keyword is mandatory on overridden methods.
127	
128	### ISP — Interface Segregation
129	- Adapter interfaces are split by capability (`PageTheatreBootAdapter`, `PageTheatrePreviewAdapter`, `PageTheatreIntroAdapter`, `PageTheatreIntroActionAdapter`, `PageTheatreSceneSyncAdapter`).
130	- Implement only the capabilities you need; the composite `PageTheatreAdapter` is optional-by-field.
131	- Do not add fields to existing interfaces just to avoid a type check — add a narrower interface.
132	
133	### DIP — Dependency Inversion
134	- `Engine` accepts `EngineDependencies` (`sceneFactory`, `modelLoaderFactory`). Use this for testing/swapping.
135	- High-level modules must not `new ConcreteClass()` mid-constructor when a factory slot exists.
136	- Cross-class lookup goes through `context.getObject(id)` (O(1)), never `scene.getObjectByName(...)` (O(n)).
137	
138	### Disposal symmetry
139	Every class that allocates is responsible for releasing:
140	
141	| Creates | Must release in `dispose()` |
142	|---|---|
143	| `addEventListener` | `removeEventListener` with same reference + options |
144	| `setTimeout` / `setInterval` | `clearTimeout` / `clearInterval` |
145	| `requestAnimationFrame` | `cancelAnimationFrame` |
146	| `new MutationObserver` / Intersection / Resize | `.disconnect()` |
147	| `THREE.BufferGeometry` | `.dispose()` |
148	| `THREE.Material` | `.dispose()` + all texture slots |
149	| `THREE.Texture` | `.dispose()` — or register via `SceneObject._ownedTextures` |
150	| `THREE.Light` | `.parent?.remove(light)` + `light.dispose?.()` + target removal |
151	| `Element.animate()` | `.cancel()` |
152	| Debounce / scheduler | `.offCancel()` |
153	| Theatre subscription | Call returned unsubscribe |
154	| Scene pub/sub subscription | Call returned unsubscribe |
155	
156	Use the helpers:
157	- `utils/disposeObject3D.ts` — traverses an Object3D, disposes geometries + materials (with all 21 texture slots + shader uniform textures).
158	- `utils/disposeObject3D.ts#removeAndDispose(node)` — detach from parent and dispose.
159	
160	### Side effects
161	- Constructors: wiring only. No DOM queries, no RAF, no fetches, no listener registration. Do it in `init()`/`mount()`.
162	- Module top-level: no side effects. No `window.addEventListener` at import time. No singletons created at import time.
163	- Static fields: no mutable state. If you need tracking (e.g., `ContactWizard._instances`), it must be reset by a static `dispose()`.
164	
165	## 5. THREE.js GPU/CPU optimization playbook
166	
167	### Render-loop hot path rules (hard bans)
168	
169	1. **No `new Vector2/Vector3/Matrix4/Quaternion/Euler` inside `runUpdate`, `render`, or any per-frame callback.**
170	   - Use module-scope or instance `_scratch` fields. Mutate with `.copy()`, `.set()`, `.applyMatrix4()`.
171	2. **No object literals inside per-frame paths.**
172	   - Cache resolved options in an instance scratch object. Recompute only when inputs change (in `setOptions`, not in `runUpdate`).
173	3. **No `scene.getObjectByName()` per frame.** Use `context.getObject(id)` (O(1) Map lookup) or subscribe via `Scene.onObjectRegistered`.
174	4. **No `new Set()` / `Object.keys()` / `Array.from()` inside hot path.** Pre-compute key arrays when source changes.
175	5. **No `.getSnapshot()` called more than once per frame.** Cache locally in the function.
176	6. **No `uniform.tX.value = texture` per frame.** Textures set once at material creation; only scalars/vectors update per frame.
177	
178	### World matrix freshness
179	
180	- Before reading `object.matrixWorld` or `object.getWorldPosition()`, call `object.updateWorldMatrix(true, false)` if the render hasn't run yet this frame.
181	- Known call sites that already do this: `Engine._resolveFollowAnchor`, `CameraTargetRuntime.resolveFollowAnchor`, `CloudPlane._applyRocketUniforms`.
182	
183	### GPU memory
184

193	- `onBeforeCompile` closures must not retain frame-local state. Store uniform refs in `userData.shader` for later mutation.
194	- `needsUpdate = true` is set exactly once (after `onBeforeCompile` assignment). Never in the render loop.

206	- Self-check: 60fps with GC events < 2/sec. Allocation profiler should show ~0 new Vector2/Vector3/Object per frame.

# TypeScript Architecture Guidelines

Source of truth for code additions/refactors in `resource/ts/`. Read this before writing new code.

> Setup-time harness checklist (CLAUDE.md sizing, hooks, allowedTools, skills config) lives in `.claude/SETUP_CHECKLIST.md`. This file is for code-writing decisions.

## 1. God objects — current state

A god object = single class mixing 3+ reasons to change or > ~600 lines of heterogeneous logic.

**Known remaining god objects (planned for separate branch decomposition):**

| File | Lines | Reason to split | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| `manager/AppManager.ts` | 1950 | Intro + showcase + UI lifecycle + contact flow + debug | Pending (plan: `lovely-humming-spindle.md` Phase 3-1) |
| `ui/ContactWizard.ts` | 1445 | Step nav + chip anim + form sync + submission | Dispose leak fixed; split pending (Phase 3-2 partial) |
| `pages/works/runtime/WorksPageRuntime.ts` | 1254 | Route lifecycle + scroll + intro + camera + wheel hints | Pending review |
| `builder/TimelineBuilder.ts` | 1007 | Declarative GSAP timeline DSL | Size justified (DSL engine) — keep |
| `pages/main/theatre/MainTheatreRuntime.ts` | 919 | Theatre sequences + sheet effects + autoplay | Phase 3-4 |
| `pages/works/render/WorksSceneManager.ts` | 825 | Layout + render + pointer + view mode | Phase 3-3 |
| `pages/about/theatre/AboutTheatreBridge.ts` | 818 | Theatre ↔ scene bindings | Review if splittable by sequence |
| `manager/BackgroundManager.ts` | 730 | Env + uniforms + transitions | Acceptable (single rendering concern) |

**Healthy coordinators (do not touch):**
- `core/Scene.ts`, `core/PageTheatreBinder.ts`, `runtime/PageRuntime.ts` — clean single-purpose orchestrators.
- All `types/*.types.ts` — 19 files organized by domain.
- All `config/*.config.ts` — constants only, no logic.

**Claude rule:** Do not grow the god objects above. New features belong in new runtime/coordinator classes next to them.

## 2. How to extend — adding a new feature

### Decision tree

```
New feature needed
│
├─ Is it a visible 3D object?           → resource/ts/objects/<env|sub|main|rocket|shared>/
│                                         Extends SceneObject<TweenProps>
│
├─ Is it DOM UI (header, modal, form)?  → resource/ts/ui/ or resource/ts/components/
│                                         Must implement init() + dispose()
│
├─ Is it page-scoped runtime state?     → resource/ts/pages/<page>/runtime/
│
├─ Is it Theatre.js binding for a page? → resource/ts/pages/<page>/theatre/
│                                         Register in PageTheatreBinder factory map
│
├─ Is it a cross-page orchestrator?     → resource/ts/runtime/ or resource/ts/manager/
│                                         Needs strong justification
│
├─ Is it a shader / material?           → resource/shaders/ + referenced from objects/
│
└─ Is it a constant / color / URL?      → resource/ts/config/<domain>.config.ts
                                          NOT inline
```

### New scene object checklist

1. File: `objects/<group>/YourObject.ts` extending `SceneObject<YourTweenProps>`.
2. Implement `runObject()`, `runUpdate(dt)`, `dispose()`, `applyVisibility()`.
3. Type: `YourObjectOptions` + `YourTweenProps` in `types/object.types.ts` (not inline).
4. Config: constants in `config/<group>.config.ts`.
5. Dispose: every allocated geometry/material/texture goes through `utils/disposeObject3D.ts` or `SceneObject._ownedTextures`.
6. Registration: `ObjectSetup.ts` for instance + optional `registerObject(id, ...)` for cross-object lookup.

### New DOM component checklist

1. File: `ui/YourComponent.ts` (singletons) or `components/YourComponent.ts` (reusable widgets).
2. Static `init({ root })` + static `dispose()` pair. If multiple instances, keep a `Set<Instance>` and iterate in `dispose()`.
3. All event listeners: store bound handlers as fields, remove the same references in `dispose()`.
4. Timers: track via `Set<number>` + helper `_trackedTimeout`. Clear all in `dispose()`.
5. Web Animations API: track via `Set<Animation>` + helper `_trackAnimation`. Cancel all in `dispose()`.
6. Hook into `PageRuntime.dispose()` so page navigation tears down cleanly.
7. Options/data types → `types/component.types.ts`.
8. CSS class names / selectors → `config/component.config.ts` or `config/dom.config.ts`.

### New page route checklist

Use `/new-route` skill. Adds:
- `routes/web.php` closure route
- `views/pages/<page>.php` view
- Optional `resource/ts/pages/<page>/` entry

## 3. Roles

| Folder | Role | What lives here | What does NOT |
|---|---|---|---|
| `core/` | Engine + scene + lifecycle primitives | `Engine`, `Scene`, `AnimationLoop`, `PostProcessor`, `ModelLoader`, `PageTheatreBinder`, `SceneObject` base | Page-specific logic |
| `runtime/` | Cross-cutting app-level state machines | `PageRuntime`, `ResponsiveRuntime`, `IntroFlowRuntime`, `ScrollSceneRuntime`, `TimelineRuntime` | Per-page scenes |
| `manager/` | Heavyweight orchestrators | `AppManager` (to be split), `BackgroundManager`, `QaManager`, `IntroManager`, `ShaderManager` | New single-responsibility code (prefer `runtime/` or `core/`) |
| `pages/<page>/runtime/` | Per-page lifecycle | Page-specific scroll, intro, interaction runtimes | Code shared across pages |
| `pages/<page>/scene/` | Per-page THREE.js scene graph wiring | Object composition specific to the page | Generic scene objects |
| `pages/<page>/theatre/` | Per-page Theatre.js bindings | `*TheatreBridge`, `*TheatreRuntime`, `*SceneState` | DOM-only logic |
| `pages/<page>/render/` | Per-page standalone renderers (rare) | `WorksSceneManager` style secondary renderers | Main engine scenes |
| `objects/` | THREE.js scene objects | Classes extending `SceneObject` | DOM elements |
| `ui/` | DOM singletons | `Header`, `Drawer`, `ContactWizard`, `WorkModal`, `IntroCanvas` | Reusable widgets (go to `components/`) |
| `components/` | Reusable DOM widgets | `Button`, `Marquee`, `CustomCursor`, `TextReveal`, `WhySkillPreview` | Scene objects |
| `animation/` | Non-GSAP DOM animation primitives | `TextReveal`, `BlockReveal` base | 3D tweens |
| `builder/` | Declarative composition engines | `TimelineBuilder` | Runtime state |
| `validation/` | Form/input validation | `ContactFormValidation` | Business logic |
| `utils/` | Pure leaf helpers | `disposeObject3D`, `Debounce`, `FrameScheduler`, `Aria`, `Helpers` | Stateful managers |
| `config/` | Constants only | colors, selectors, durations, URLs | Any logic |
| `types/` | Type definitions only | `*.types.ts` per domain | Runtime code |
| `app/` | Bootstrap entry | `AppBootstrap`, `ObjectSetup`, `EnvSetup` | Feature code |
| `lib/` | Third-party wrappers | Theatre.js, Lenis wrappers | Domain code |

Every file must fit one row. If it fits none, stop and reconsider the design.

## 4. OOP / SOLID checklist for new code

Run through this list mentally before writing the class.

### SRP — Single Responsibility
- One "reason to change" per class. If you need "and" to describe it, split.
- If > 400 lines, ask whether 2+ smaller classes fit better.
- **New code must not be added to `AppManager` or `ContactWizard`.** Extend in a sibling class.

### OCP — Open/Closed
- New page variants → add to factory map (`PageTheatreBinder.PAGE_THEATRE_ADAPTER_FACTORIES`), never a new `if (pageId === ...)` branch.
- New light/object types → register in a creator map (`SceneLights._creators` pattern), never a switch.
- Use the `ObjectFactoryRegistry` for new scene-object kinds.

### LSP — Liskov Substitution
- Subclasses of `SceneObject` must respect the contract: `init` → `runObject` → `runUpdate` → `dispose`, no partial cycles.
- `override` keyword is mandatory on overridden methods.

### ISP — Interface Segregation
- Adapter interfaces are split by capability (`PageTheatreBootAdapter`, `PageTheatrePreviewAdapter`, `PageTheatreIntroAdapter`, `PageTheatreIntroActionAdapter`, `PageTheatreSceneSyncAdapter`).
- Implement only the capabilities you need; the composite `PageTheatreAdapter` is optional-by-field.
- Do not add fields to existing interfaces just to avoid a type check — add a narrower interface.

### DIP — Dependency Inversion
- `Engine` accepts `EngineDependencies` (`sceneFactory`, `modelLoaderFactory`). Use this for testing/swapping.
- High-level modules must not `new ConcreteClass()` mid-constructor when a factory slot exists.
- Cross-class lookup goes through `context.getObject(id)` (O(1)), never `scene.getObjectByName(...)` (O(n)).

### Disposal symmetry
Every class that allocates is responsible for releasing:

| Creates | Must release in `dispose()` |
|---|---|
| `addEventListener` | `removeEventListener` with same reference + options |
| `setTimeout` / `setInterval` | `clearTimeout` / `clearInterval` |
| `requestAnimationFrame` | `cancelAnimationFrame` |
| `new MutationObserver` / Intersection / Resize | `.disconnect()` |
| `THREE.BufferGeometry` | `.dispose()` |
| `THREE.Material` | `.dispose()` + all texture slots |
| `THREE.Texture` | `.dispose()` — or register via `SceneObject._ownedTextures` |
| `THREE.Light` | `.parent?.remove(light)` + `light.dispose?.()` + target removal |
| `Element.animate()` | `.cancel()` |
| Debounce / scheduler | `.offCancel()` |
| Theatre subscription | Call returned unsubscribe |
| Scene pub/sub subscription | Call returned unsubscribe |

Use the helpers:
- `utils/disposeObject3D.ts` — traverses an Object3D, disposes geometries + materials (with all 21 texture slots + shader uniform textures).
- `utils/disposeObject3D.ts#removeAndDispose(node)` — detach from parent and dispose.

### Side effects
- Constructors: wiring only. No DOM queries, no RAF, no fetches, no listener registration. Do it in `init()`/`mount()`.
- Module top-level: no side effects. No `window.addEventListener` at import time. No singletons created at import time.
- Static fields: no mutable state. If you need tracking (e.g., `ContactWizard._instances`), it must be reset by a static `dispose()`.

## 5. THREE.js GPU/CPU optimization playbook

### Render-loop hot path rules (hard bans)

1. **No `new Vector2/Vector3/Matrix4/Quaternion/Euler` inside `runUpdate`, `render`, or any per-frame callback.**
   - Use module-scope or instance `_scratch` fields. Mutate with `.copy()`, `.set()`, `.applyMatrix4()`.
2. **No object literals inside per-frame paths.**
   - Cache resolved options in an instance scratch object. Recompute only when inputs change (in `setOptions`, not in `runUpdate`).
3. **No `scene.getObjectByName()` per frame.** Use `context.getObject(id)` (O(1) Map lookup) or subscribe via `Scene.onObjectRegistered`.
4. **No `new Set()` / `Object.keys()` / `Array.from()` inside hot path.** Pre-compute key arrays when source changes.
5. **No `.getSnapshot()` called more than once per frame.** Cache locally in the function.
6. **No `uniform.tX.value = texture` per frame.** Textures set once at material creation; only scalars/vectors update per frame.

### World matrix freshness

- Before reading `object.matrixWorld` or `object.getWorldPosition()`, call `object.updateWorldMatrix(true, false)` if the render hasn't run yet this frame.
- Known call sites that already do this: `Engine._resolveFollowAnchor`, `CameraTargetRuntime.resolveFollowAnchor`, `CloudPlane._applyRocketUniforms`.

### GPU memory

- Every cached model must be cloned with independent materials. `ModelLoader.loadGLTF` handles this via `_cloneMaterialsInPlace` — don't bypass.
- Shader swaps on cached meshes must guard against re-application. Use `userData.__<name>Applied` tag (see `Ground._applyGroundShader`).
- On page teardown: `Engine.dispose()` → `Scene.dispose()` → every `SceneObject.dispose()` → `disposeObject3D(timelineRoot)`.
- Secondary renderers (like `WorksSceneManager`): must call `renderer.dispose()` AND `renderer.forceContextLoss()`.

### Materials / shaders

- Clone materials before mutation to avoid cache pollution: `material.clone()`.
- `onBeforeCompile` closures must not retain frame-local state. Store uniform refs in `userData.shader` for later mutation.
- `needsUpdate = true` is set exactly once (after `onBeforeCompile` assignment). Never in the render loop.

### Post-processing

- `EffectComposer.setSize(w, h)` receives CSS pixels (composer applies pixel ratio internally).
- `UnrealBloomPass.resolution.set(w, h)` receives CSS pixels (matches composer).
- Do not call `renderer.setSize()` inside the render loop. Use a resize listener → `ResponsiveRuntime` dispatch.

### Profiling

- Chrome DevTools Performance → look for frames > 16.67ms and GC sawteeth.
- `chrome://tracing` / WebGL Inspector for draw-call counts.
- Self-check: 60fps with GC events < 2/sec. Allocation profiler should show ~0 new Vector2/Vector3/Object per frame.

## 6. Responsive architecture

The project centralizes all responsive state through `ResponsiveRuntime` (pub/sub). Build new responsive features on top of it; do not add ad-hoc `window.matchMedia` listeners.

### Contract

```ts
const runtime = ResponsiveRuntime.getDefault();
const snapshot = runtime.getSnapshot();
// snapshot.breakpoint: "sm" | "md" | "lg" | "xl"
// snapshot.viewportWidth / viewportHeight
// snapshot.render.clampedPixelRatio
// snapshot.device.isMobile
// snapshot.reducedMotion
// snapshot.performance tier

const unsubscribe = runtime.subscribe((next) => {
  // react to breakpoint / viewport / reduced motion changes
});
// In dispose(): unsubscribe();
```

### Extension rules

- **New responsive value:** derive from `snapshot` inside the consumer. Don't add fields to `ResponsiveSnapshot` unless multiple consumers need it.
- **Config with breakpoint variance:** use `utils/ResponsiveValue.ts` (`{ sm, md, lg, xl, default }`) — declare in `config/`, resolve at call site.
- **Reduced motion:** check `snapshot.reducedMotion` and provide a degraded path (no infinite loops, no parallax). Required for accessibility.
- **Pixel ratio / performance tier:** read `snapshot.render.clampedPixelRatio` and `snapshot.performance` — used by `Engine` and `PostProcessor` automatically. Pass the snapshot through, don't re-derive.
- **Orientation / mobile only:** prefer `snapshot.device.isMobile` over UA sniffing.
- **Three.js resizing:** single path. Resize listener → `ResponsiveRuntime.updateFromWindow()` → subscribers (`Engine.applyResponsiveSnapshot`, `PostProcessor.resize`, `WorksSceneManager`). Do not bind `window.resize` in new code.

### CSS integration

- `ResponsiveRuntime._applyCssVariables(snapshot)` publishes CSS custom properties. Read them in SCSS via `var(--vw, 1vw)` etc., not through JS-computed inline styles.

### Touch vs hover

- Hover UX (`mouseenter` / `mouseleave`) stays on `MouseEvent` semantics — it's desktop-only by design.
- Drag / press / click target → `PointerEvent` (`pointerdown` / `pointerup` / `pointermove`) with `pointerId` tracking. See `CustomCursor` and `WorksPageRuntime` patterns.

### Anti-patterns (do not ship)

- Inline `@media` in TypeScript conditions (`if (window.innerWidth < 768)`). Use the snapshot.
- `matchMedia` listener per component. Use `ResponsiveRuntime.subscribe`.
- Hardcoded breakpoint numbers in TS. Source them from `config/` or from `snapshot.breakpoint`.
- Fighting against `prefers-reduced-motion` (autoplay, infinite animations). Respect it.

75	## Permission setup — `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions`
76	
77	To prevent Claude Code from asking for permission on every action, enable via VS Code:
78	
79	1. Open **File → Preferences → Settings** (or `Ctrl+,`)
80	2. Search for `claudeCode.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions`
81	3. Check the box — this adds "Bypass permissions" to the mode cycle
82	
83	> **Warning:** This flag auto-approves all tool use: file writes, Bash execution, etc.
84	> Use only in trusted projects. Default permission mode is recommended for unfamiliar codebases.

87	
88	`npm run build`, `npm run watch`, and `npm install` are **forbidden during normal development**.
89	
90	- **Reason:** Vite dev server at `http://localhost:8888` auto-rebuilds the bundle on every file save
91	- Running these wastes context and time with no benefit
92	- **Exception:** `npm install <package>` — only when explicitly adding a new dependency
93	- This rule lives in two places: `AGENTS.md` (cross-AI canonical) and `.claude/rules/frontend.md` (Claude auto-load on `.ts`/`.tsx` edits). CLAUDE.md inherits via `@AGENTS.md` import.
94

96	
97	When a `.ts` file is modified via the Edit or Write tool, the PostToolUse hook fires automatically:
98	
99	```bash
100	# Command executed by the hook
101	rtk tsc --noEmit
102	```
103	
104	- Hook config: `.claude/settings.json` → `PostToolUse` → matcher: `Edit|Write`
105	- If tsc errors are found, the hook returns `exit(1)`, immediately notifying Claude
106	- **How to verify:** Edit any `.ts` file with the Edit tool → check hook output for tsc results

- [ ] `rtk gain` count increasing? Zero means rtk is not actually being used.

---

## Current project setup status

| Item | Status |
| --- | --- |
| CLAUDE.md concise | ✅ |
| CLAUDE.md skill invocation examples | ✅ |
| Rules on-demand | ✅ php / frontend / scss |
| Hooks (tsc) | ✅ Node.js stdin pattern |
| Hook verified | ✅ Confirmed firing via Edit tool on .ts file |
| allowedTools | ✅ rtk / git / tsc / docker / npm test |
| Skills | ✅ migration / new-route |
| Subagents | ✅ scene-explorer / php-explorer |
| docs/ removed + README cleaned | ✅ |
| spatie/image WEBP optimization | ✅ 1.10.6 (PHP 7.4 compat), ImageProcessor, dockerfile libwebp-dev |
| RTK applied | ✅ (WSL Remote = auto-rewrite hook; native Windows = explicit `rtk` prefix) |
| MEMORY.md | ✅ architecture / workflow / rtk / npm / permissions |
| Test framework | ✅ vitest (19 tests) |
| --dangerously-skip-permissions | ✅ VS Code setting (allowDangerouslySkipPermissions) |
| npm build/watch/install forbidden | ✅ AGENTS.md / frontend.md (CLAUDE.md inherits via @AGENTS.md) |
| All AI-read files in English | ✅ |

## Permission setup — `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions`

To prevent Claude Code from asking for permission on every action, enable via VS Code:

1. Open **File → Preferences → Settings** (or `Ctrl+,`)
2. Search for `claudeCode.allowDangerouslySkipPermissions`
3. Check the box — this adds "Bypass permissions" to the mode cycle

> **Warning:** This flag auto-approves all tool use: file writes, Bash execution, etc.
> Use only in trusted projects. Default permission mode is recommended for unfamiliar codebases.

## Why npm build commands are forbidden

`npm run build`, `npm run watch`, and `npm install` are **forbidden during normal development**.

- **Reason:** Vite dev server at `http://localhost:8888` auto-rebuilds the bundle on every file save
- Running these wastes context and time with no benefit
- **Exception:** `npm install <package>` — only when explicitly adding a new dependency
- This rule lives in two places: `AGENTS.md` (cross-AI canonical) and `.claude/rules/frontend.md` (Claude auto-load on `.ts`/`.tsx` edits). CLAUDE.md inherits via `@AGENTS.md` import.

## How the tsc PostToolUse hook works

When a `.ts` file is modified via the Edit or Write tool, the PostToolUse hook fires automatically:

```bash
# Command executed by the hook
rtk tsc --noEmit
```

- Hook config: `.claude/settings.json` → `PostToolUse` → matcher: `Edit|Write`
- If tsc errors are found, the hook returns `exit(1)`, immediately notifying Claude
- **How to verify:** Edit any `.ts` file with the Edit tool → check hook output for tsc results

# Part B — Working With Claude

Operational playbook for the human ↔ Claude loop. Part A (above) governs *what* code looks like; Part B governs *how* the session is run.

## 1. Plan-first cycle

Use `Shift+Tab` (or `/plan`) to enter Plan Mode before any change that:
- modifies 2+ files, OR
- touches an unfamiliar subsystem, OR
- you cannot describe in one sentence as a diff.

Plan files land in `~/.claude/plans/<slug>.md`. Review and edit the plan there before approving.

Skip Plan Mode for: typo fixes, single-line tweaks, copy edits, doc-only updates with obvious scope. Time-box exploration — if a plan keeps growing, stop and ask the user instead.

Cycle: **Explore → Plan → Implement → Verify → Commit.** Each phase has a clean exit; do not interleave.

## 2. Course-correct protocol

Tight feedback beats long debugging. When Claude goes off-track:

| Failure count | Action |
|---|---|
| 1st | Reply with a corrective prompt naming the specific mistake |
| 2nd | `Esc Esc` or `/rewind` to a checkpoint before the wrong turn — do **not** keep correcting |
| 3rd+ | `/clear`, then restart with a tighter prompt that incorporates what you learned |

Across sessions: `claude --continue` resumes the latest, `claude --resume` picks from history. `/rename <slug>` makes long-running work findable.

A polluted context is worse than a fresh one. If you've corrected the same issue twice, the failed attempts are now in scope and Claude will repeat them.

## 3. Context hygiene

Context is the scarce resource — protect it.

- `/clear` between unrelated tasks. Always. The cost of re-priming context is lower than the cost of distraction.
- `/compact <focus>` when a single long task fills the window — Claude summarizes around your stated focus.
- **Delegate to explorer agents** for any read-heavy investigation:
  - Three.js / `resource/ts/`: `$scene-explorer`
  - Routes / views / admin / schema: `$php-explorer`
  - General codebase sweeps: `Explore` subagent (`Glob`/`Grep`/`Read` only)
- Never load >500-line files into the main context if an explorer agent can answer the question.
- The PostToolUse `tsc` hook (`.claude/settings.json`) handles type-check noise — do not re-run it manually.

## 4. Parallel workflows

Claude scales horizontally. Use it.

- **Independent investigations** → fire 2+ explorer agents in a single message (parallel tool calls). Example: `$scene-explorer` for runtime ownership + `$php-explorer` for the matching API endpoint.
- **Writer/Reviewer split** for risky changes: one session implements; a fresh session reviews the diff. The reviewer has no prior bias toward the code it just wrote.
- **Test/Implement split**: have one session write Vitest cases, a second session make them pass. Pairs well with TDD (see Verification rules in `AGENTS.md`).
- Avoid spawning subagents for tasks the main session can finish in 1–2 tool calls — overhead exceeds savings.

## 5. When in doubt

- Verbose context > vague prompt: paste error output, name file paths, point to existing patterns to mimic.
- If you are about to type "and also...", stop — that's a separate task. `/clear` first.
- Trust the hook. If `tsc` did not complain, do not re-run it.

## How the tsc PostToolUse hook works

When a `.ts` file is modified via the Edit or Write tool, the PostToolUse hook fires automatically:

```bash
# Command executed by the hook
rtk tsc --noEmit
```

- Hook config: `.claude/settings.json` → `PostToolUse` → matcher: `Edit|Write`
- If tsc errors are found, the hook returns `exit(1)`, immediately notifying Claude
- **How to verify:** Edit any `.ts` file with the Edit tool → check hook output for tsc results

## How the tsc PostToolUse hook works

When a `.ts` file is modified via the Edit or Write tool, the PostToolUse hook fires automatically:

```bash
# Command executed by the hook
rtk tsc --noEmit
```

- Hook config: `.claude/settings.json` → `PostToolUse` → matcher: `Edit|Write`
- If tsc errors are found, the hook returns `exit(1)`, immediately notifying Claude
- **How to verify:** Edit any `.ts` file with the Edit tool → check hook output for tsc results

## 8. Permission strategy

Three layers, pick the lightest one that still keeps you in the loop.

| Mode | When | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowDangerouslySkipPermissions` | Trusted local repo work (current default) | VS Code setting — already enabled, see §"Permission setup" above |
| `/permissions` allowlist | Untrusted code, external PR review, shared boxes | Run `/permissions` and approve specific tools (`rtk git *`, `rtk tsc`, etc.) instead of blanket bypass |
| Default prompt-per-action | First time on a strange branch, when investigating supply-chain risk | No flag — Claude asks before each Bash/MCP call |

Rules of thumb:
- **Never** add a tool to the global allowlist that can write outside the repo (e.g., `rm -rf /`, `aws *`). Keep blast radius local.
- New MCP server: `claude mcp add <name>` then verify entry in `.claude/settings.json`. Document the why in this file before committing.
- `gh` CLI is preferred over raw GitHub API — it handles auth, avoids rate limits, and keeps PR/issue work out of the browser. Install with `winget install --id GitHub.cli` if missing.
- Forbidden flags regardless of mode: `--no-verify`, `--no-gpg-sign`, `git push --force` to `main`. Hooks and signatures are not optional.

# Claude Code Harness Setup Checklist

One-time setup health check for the Claude Code harness in this project. Code-writing guidelines live in `.claude/BEST_PRACTICES.md`.

---

## 1. CLAUDE.md

- [x] Under 50 lines? — Yes (post-2026-04-25 slim)
- [x] Does not contain anything Claude can infer from reading the code (file structure, naming conventions, etc.)?
- [x] File-type rules are separated into `.claude/rules/`?
- [x] Explicit "do not" prohibition patterns listed?
- [x] Verification commands included (tsc, lint, test, etc.)?

## 2. Rules (`.claude/rules/`)

- [x] Split by file extension? (`php.md`, `frontend.md`, `scss.md`)
- [x] Each rules file has a `paths:` frontmatter header?
- [x] Rules contain only things that cannot be inferred from the code?

## 3. Hooks (`.claude/settings.json`)

- [x] Auto-runs tsc after editing a `.ts` file?
